passage: Transcript: So most of the world's earthquakes are not scattered at random. If you plot them on a map, they line up, they trace the edges of the tectonic plates. And that's the clue to what causes them. The Earth's outer shell is broken into these giant plates, and they're slowly moving, a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Where two plates meet, you get a boundary, and there are three basic kinds. At a divergent boundary, plates pull apart, and new crust wells up, think mid-ocean ridges. At a convergent boundary, they push together, and one plate may dive beneath the other. And at a transform boundary, they grind past each other sideways, the San Andreas Fault is the classic example. Now here's the mechanism for the quakes. The plates don't slide smoothly. They lock, friction holds them in place, and stress builds up over years, decades. Then, at some point, the rock can't take it, it slips suddenly, and all that stored energy releases as seismic waves. That's the earthquake. So the shaking you feel is really the sudden release of stress that had been accumulating quietly the whole time along that boundary.

However — and this trips people up every year — the upper floors, including the quiet reading room and the special collections, still close at midnight. So if you're pulling an all-nighter, plan to be on the main floor after twelve. A couple of practical notes. Overnight, entry is card-access only; you'll need to tap your student ID at the side door, since the main entrance locks at eleven. And we've added a rule this year: after midnight, the group study rooms switch to a ninety-minute limit, no back-to-back bookings, so that everyone gets a fair shot during crunch time. Free coffee will be available in the lobby from ten p.m. onward, courtesy of the student union. Please, be considerate of others who are trying to focus.

passage: Transcript: Hi, everyone. I want to tell you about an event next Thursday that I think a lot of you won't want to miss. The department is hosting Ana Delgado, the documentary filmmaker — some of you may have seen her film on urban water systems — for an evening talk in Hale Auditorium at seven p.m. Now, a few things. This is not a screening; she's speaking about how she funds and researches her projects, which, if you're thinking about documentary work, is honestly more useful than watching another film. Seating is limited to about two hundred, and here's the important part: you do need a ticket, but tickets are free. You reserve one through the department's events page, and I'd do it soon — last year's speaker filled up in two days. If you reserve a ticket and then can't make it, please release it online so someone on the waitlist can grab it. Oh, and she's agreed to stay afterward for a smaller Q and A session, but that part is first-come, first-served in the seminar room next door — no separate ticket, just show up.

passage: Transcript: Good evening, everyone. This is a reminder from the Office of Residence Life about our annual fire-safety inspection, which will take place next Wednesday and Thursday. Inspectors from the university's safety office will enter every room in all four residence halls, so you do not need to be present, but your room must be accessible. Please make sure walkways are clear and that nothing is blocking the door or the window. A few things they'll be checking for: first, no candles, incense, or open flames of any kind — these are the most common reason a room fails. Second, extension cords and power strips must be the surge-protected type; the flat white cords many of you brought from home are not permitted. Third, the smoke detector in your room must be uncovered and unobstructed. If you've hung anything from it, take that down before Wednesday. Rooms that fail will be re-inspected the following week, and a second failure carries a fifty-dollar fine. If you have questions, email the front desk — please don't call after nine p.m. Thank you.

passage: Transcript: Hi, students. This is an important update from the Registrar's Office about course registration for the spring term. In previous years, the deadline to add or drop a class fell in the third week of the semester. Beginning this spring, that window is closing much sooner: you now have until the end of the first week only. We made this change because too many students were dropping courses in week three, which left classmates unable to plan group projects and left instructors with unstable rosters. So mark your calendar — Friday, January thirtieth, is the final day to make any schedule changes without a penalty. After that date, dropping a course will show up on your transcript as a withdrawal, and adding a course will require the instructor's written signature. One more thing: the online registration system will be offline for maintenance this Saturday, so plan to finalize your schedule either before Saturday or on Sunday. If you're on a waitlist, keep checking your email, since spots open up quickly in the first few days. Good luck this term.
